tables.title: Figure 2. (a) Average marginal causal effect (AMCE) for each preference.
tables.population: Not explicitly stated; inferred from context as general population used in Moral Machine study
notes: In each row, ΔPr is the difference the probability of sparing characters possessing the attribute on the right, and the probability of sparing characters possessing the attribute on the left, aggregated over all other attributes.
For example (age) the probability of sparing young characters is 0.49 (SE = 0.0008) greater than the probability of sparing older characters.
The 95% CIs of the means are omitted due to their insignificant width, given the sample size.

For the number of characters (No. characters), effect sizes are shown for each number of additional characters (1 to 4); the effect size for 2 additional characters overlaps with the mean effect of the attribute.
(b) Relative advantage or penalty for each character, compared to an adult man or woman.
For each character, ΔPr is the difference between the probability of sparing this character (when presented alone) and the probability of sparing an adult man or woman.
For example, the probability of sparing a girl is 0.15 (SE = 0.003) higher than the probability of sparing an adult man/woman.

observations: Figure 2(a) shows AMCEs for binary attribute preferences across 9 categories; bars indicate ΔPr values ranging approximately from 0 to +0.8.
Figure 2(b) shows relative ΔPr for 18 individual character types vs. adult man/woman baseline; values range roughly from -0.2 to +0.2.
Icons accompany each attribute/character label (e.g., human figures, animals, symbols).
The text below the figure explains interpretation of ΔPr and notes omission of 95% CIs due to narrow width.

The paragraph following the figure states: 'Policymakers cannot solely rely on global trends when assessing social expectations... If these conditions are not met, then policymakers should be aware of individual and national variations in the preferences extracted from the Moral Machine.'
uncertainties: Exact numerical ΔPr values are not transcribed because they are only visible as bar lengths in figures, not as explicit numbers in table format.
Standard errors (SE) are provided only for two examples (age: SE=0.0008; girl: SE=0.003), but not for other rows/characters.
Population definition is not explicitly stated in the figure or caption.

The phrase 'effect sizes are shown for each number of additional characters (1 to 4)' implies multiple data points for 'No. Characters', but only one label ('Sparring Fewer Characters' / 'Sparring More Characters') is listed per row; exact mapping of 1–4 additional characters to specific ΔPr values is not provided in tabular form.
Figure 2(b) axis labels show ΔPr scale from -0.2 to +0.2, but precise values for each character are not numerically listed—only visual bar positions.
